claim: The M2 is categorized as the dorsomedial PFC in rodents based on its anatomical features, including thalamocortical and cortical–basal ganglia connections, and its functional role in motor decision.
source: The M2 is categorized as the dorsomedial PFC in rodents in some publications, based on both its anatomical features, including thalamocortical and cortical–basal ganglia connections, and its functional role in motor decision (Sul et al., 2011; Uylings et al., 2003; Hoover and Vertes, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Sul et al., 2011; Uylings et al., 2003; Hoover and Vertes, 2007).

claim: The M2 receives inputs from both the VTA and the secondary visual cortex lateral area (V2L).
source: The M2 receives inputs from both the VTA and the secondary visual cortex lateral area (V2L) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A,B showing retrograde and anterograde tracing data.

claim: Fluorogold injected into the PFC labels cells in the V2L.
source: Fluorogold was injected into the prefrontal cortex (PFC). Cells in the secondary visual cortex lateral area (V2L) were labeled.
evidence: The claim is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FITC-dextran injected into the V2L results in labeled fibers observed in the PFC.
source: FITC-dextran was injected into the V2L. Labeled fibers were observed in the PFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by the anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most DA neurons are spontaneously active with firing patterns that range from regular tonic firing (1–5 Hz) to phasic firing (40–50 Hz).
source: Most DA neurons are spontaneously active with firing patterns that range from regular tonic firing (1–5 Hz) to phasic firing (40–50 Hz) (Robinson et al., 2004; Grace and Bunney, 1984a; Grace and Bunney, 1984b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Robinson et al., 2004; Grace and Bunney, 1984a; Grace and Bunney, 1984b).

claim: Salient events such as experiencing a novel environment or receiving a reward-associated signal evoke phasic firing in the VTA.
source: In addition, salient events such as experiencing a novel environment or receiving a reward-associated signal, evoke phasic firing in the VTA (Schultz, 2007; Horvitz, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Schultz, 2007; Horvitz, 2000).

claim: Low frequency VTA microstimulation (1 Hz–10 Hz, tonic range) evokes Ca2+ transients in PFC neurons that decay within 5 s.
source: When low frequency VTA microstimulation was used (1 Hz–10 Hz, tonic range), Ca2+ transients in the PFC neurons were evoked and decayed within 5 s.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The steep increase and short decay of Ca2+ transients from low frequency VTA stimulation is comparable with the reported response to sensory input observed in cortical neurons of anesthetized animals.
source: This steep increase and short decay is comparable with the reported response to sensory input observed in cortical neurons of anesthetized animals (Ohki et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Ohki et al., 2005).

claim: High frequency VTA stimulation (40–50 Hz, phasic range) evokes substantially elongated Ca2+ transients that last 20–30 s and then return to the original baseline.
source: In contrast, high frequency VTA stimulation (40–50 Hz, phasic range) evoked substantially elongated Ca2+ transients that lasted 20–30 s and then returned to the original baseline (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ca2+ transients of PFC neurons in response to high frequency VTA stimulation reach a peak relatively slowly, 6–7 s after stimulation.
source: In addition, these Ca2+ transients of the PFC neurons reached a peak relatively slowly, 6–7 s after stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: High frequency VTA stimulation robustly evokes Ca2+ transients in all tested animals.
source: Furthermore, high frequency VTA stimulation robustly evoked Ca2+ transients in all tested animals, whereas low frequency VTA stimulation did not as only about half of the animals tested showed detectable Ca2+ transients in the PFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Low frequency VTA stimulation evokes detectable Ca2+ transients in only about half of the animals tested.
source: Furthermore, high frequency VTA stimulation robustly evoked Ca2+ transients in all tested animals, whereas low frequency VTA stimulation did not as only about half of the animals tested showed detectable Ca2+ transients in the PFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Long-lasting Ca2+ transients are only detected in awake and not in anesthetized mice.
source: Importantly, these long-lasting Ca2+ transients were only detected in awake and not in anesthetized mice (Figure 1E,F), possibly because of the potential inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels by isoflurane (Herring et al., 2009; Study, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Isoflurane potentially inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: Importantly, these long-lasting Ca2+ transients were only detected in awake and not in anesthetized mice (Figure 1E,F), possibly because of the potential inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels by isoflurane (Herring et al., 2009; Study, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Herring et al., 2009; Study, 1994) and is presented as a possible explanation.

claim: V2L stimulation at all frequencies (1–50 Hz) evokes only short Ca2+ transients in PFC neurons.
source: Both stimulation frequencies only evoked short Ca2+ transients in PFC neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Input from the VTA, especially through high frequency, phasic stimulation, can induce a specific signal required to evoke long-lasting Ca2+ transients in PFC neurons.
source: Input from the VTA, especially through high frequency, phasic stimulation can therefore induce a specific signal required to evoke long-lasting Ca2+ transients in PFC neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of VTA and V2L stimulation effects described in the text.

claim: Phasic stimulation of the VTA facilitates DA release from its terminals.
source: Phasic stimulation of the VTA is known to facilitate DA release from its terminals (Tsai et al., 2009; Lavin et al., 2005), therefore, it was hypothesized that DA receptors are involved in induction of the long-lasting Ca2+ transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tsai et al., 2009; Lavin et al., 2005).

claim: DA receptors are members of the G-protein coupled receptor family and are composed of two groups: D1 and D2, which have opposing effects on intracellular signaling.
source: DA receptors are members of the G-protein coupled receptor family and are composed of two groups: D1 and D2, which have opposing effects on intracellular signaling (Seamans and Yang, 2004; Soltani et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Seamans and Yang, 2004; Soltani et al., 2013).

claim: Treatment with the D1 antagonist SCH23390 (1 mg/kg) reduces the long-lasting Ca2+ transients by 50%.
source: Treatment with the D1 antagonist SCH23390 (1 mg/kg) reduced the long-lasting Ca2+ transients by 50% and the decay time constant by 60%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Treatment with the D1 antagonist SCH23390 (1 mg/kg) reduces the decay time constant by 60%.
source: Treatment with the D1 antagonist SCH23390 (1 mg/kg) reduced the long-lasting Ca2+ transients by 50% and the decay time constant by 60%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: No detectable attenuation of long-lasting Ca2+ transients is observed in mice treated with the D2 antagonist eticlopride (0.5 mg/kg).
source: In contrast, no detectable attenuation was observed in mice treated with the D2 antagonist eticlopride (0.5 mg/kg) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The short Ca2+ response evoked by 5 Hz VTA stimulation is not affected by the D1 or D2 antagonist.
source: In addition, the short Ca2+ response evoked by a 5 Hz VTA stimulation was not affected by the D1 or D2 antagonist (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The short Ca2+ response evoked by 5 Hz VTA stimulation is reduced by NMDA and AMPA antagonists.
source: However, this short Ca2+ response was reduced by NMDA and AMPA antagonists (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: In the VTA, up to 65% of the neurons are dopaminergic and the others are GABAergic or glutamatergic.
source: In the VTA, up to 65% of the neurons are dopaminergic and the others are GABAergic or glutamatergic (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Gorelova et al., 2012), and some DA neurons co-release glutamate (Hnasko et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Gorelova et al., 2012).

claim: Some DA neurons co-release glutamate.
source: In the VTA, up to 65% of the neurons are dopaminergic and the others are GABAergic or glutamatergic (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Gorelova et al., 2012), and some DA neurons co-release glutamate (Hnasko et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hnasko et al., 2010).

claim: Glutamatergic terminals are dominant in the mesocortical pathway.
source: However, glutamatergic terminals are dominant in the mesocortical pathway (Gorelova et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Gorelova et al., 2012).

claim: Inhibition of the short Ca2+ response by glutamate receptor antagonists suggests that glutamatergic neurons contribute to the 5 Hz responses.
source: Inhibition of the short Ca2+ response by glutamate receptor antagonists suggests that glutamatergic neurons contribute to the 5 Hz responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results with glutamate receptor antagonists.

claim: Long-lasting Ca2+ transients are not affected by NMDA and AMPA antagonists.
source: However, the long-lasting Ca2+ transients were not affected by NMDA and AMPA antagonists (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The long-sustained increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration is not mediated by glutamatergic local recurrent networks.
source: This result further suggests that the long-sustained increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration is not mediated by glutamatergic local recurrent networks.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of NMDA and AMPA antagonists on long-lasting Ca2+ transients.

claim: D1 receptors are mainly involved in the long-lasting Ca2+ response in PFC neurons.
source: Over all, pharmacological experiments clearly suggest D1 receptors are mainly involved in the long-lasting Ca2+ response in PFC neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the pharmacological experiments described in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: T1 conditioning significantly increases the dF/F value more than other conditioning paradigms.
source: T1 conditioning significantly increased the dF/F value more than other conditioning paradigms, indicating that T1 conditioning has the largest modification effect on the PFC response to a sensory input (one-way ANOVA: F(3,28) = 6.504, p = 0.0018; post hoc Ryan's test: p < 0.01; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: T1 conditioning has the largest modification effect on the PFC response to a sensory input.
source: T1 conditioning significantly increased the dF/F value more than other conditioning paradigms, indicating that T1 conditioning has the largest modification effect on the PFC response to a sensory input (one-way ANOVA: F(3,28) = 6.504, p = 0.0018; post hoc Ryan's test: p < 0.01; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical analysis of dF/F values.

claim: The increase in dF/F value in T1 conditioning is due to an increased number of neurons showing high dF/F values.
source: This increase in value is due to an increased number of neurons showing high dF/F values (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is no significant correlation between the Ca2+ level in response to VTA stimulation (at conditioning) and the increased Ca2+ level in response to V2L stimulation '2 hr after' T1 conditioning.
source: In addition, there was no significant correlation between the Ca2+ level in response to VTA stimulation (at conditioning) and the increased Ca2+ level in response to V2L stimulation '2 hr after' T1 conditioning (test phase) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the increased neuronal response with V2L stimulation is independent of how well the neuron responds to the DA input.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increased neuronal response with V2L stimulation is independent of how well the neuron responds to the DA input.
source: In addition, there was no significant correlation between the Ca2+ level in response to VTA stimulation (at conditioning) and the increased Ca2+ level in response to V2L stimulation '2 hr after' T1 conditioning (test phase) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the increased neuronal response with V2L stimulation is independent of how well the neuron responds to the DA input.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of correlation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The network dynamics of the PFC microcircuit are composed of inhibitory and excitatory neurons, both of which express DA receptors.
source: This relatively unexpected conclusion may be explained by the fact that the network dynamics of the PFC microcircuit are composed of inhibitory and excitatory neurons, both of which express DA receptors.
evidence: The claim is presented as an explanation based on established knowledge about PFC circuitry.

claim: The cosine similarity in T1 is significantly increased in '2 hr after' compared with 'before'.
source: Post hoc tests also showed that the cosine similarity in T1 was significantly increased in '2 hr after' compared with 'before' (Ryan's test, p < 0.01; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in cosine similarity in T1 conditioning is not simply due to an increased number of high dF/F neurons.
source: This increase in cosine similarity in T1 conditioning is not simply due to an increased number of high dF/F neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), because '1 hr after' in T1 conditioning had a significantly increased cosine similarity (Figure 4D) but its population probability distribution was not significantly different from that of VTA only (2 hr after) or T2 (2 hr after) (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.5128 and p = 0.1418, respectively) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing cosine similarity and population distributions.

claim: The increased cosine similarity is not due to increased reliability of Ca2+ transients occurrence in response to three repetitive V2L stimulations.
source: In addition, the increased cosine similarity was not due to increased reliability of Ca2+ transients occurrence in response to three repetitive V2L stimulations, because the reliability calculated by Cronbach's alpha did not change between 'before' and '2 hr after' in any of the conditioning groups, including T1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only T1 conditioning improves the pattern similarity in PFC neurons.
source: These results indicate that only T1 conditioning improved the pattern similarity in PFC neurons, and the increase in pattern similarity could be the result of circuit (network) modification, and not simply the result of increased reliability of Ca2+ transients occurrence or an increased number of high responding dF/F neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results described in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increase in pattern similarity could be the result of circuit (network) modification.
source: These results indicate that only T1 conditioning improved the pattern similarity in PFC neurons, and the increase in pattern similarity could be the result of circuit (network) modification, and not simply the result of increased reliability of Ca2+ transients occurrence or an increased number of high responding dF/F neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and presented as a possible explanation.

claim: Only coincident visual sensory input with long-lasting Ca2+ transients increases neuronal activity and induces robust repeatable neuronal responses, at the population level, to the same sensory input.
source: This study revealed that only coincident visual sensory input with long-lasting Ca2+ transients increased neuronal activity and induced robust repeatable neuronal responses, at the population level, to the same sensory input.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: By increasing both dF/F and pattern similarity, DA input may enhance PFC activity and establish cortical representation.
source: By increasing both dF/F and pattern similarity, DA input may enhance PFC activity and establish cortical representation (Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation to published literature (Xue et al., 2010).

claim: DA release plays a major role in dynamic cortical remodeling in the auditory cortex.
source: In fact, it is known that DA release plays a major role in dynamic cortical remodeling in the auditory cortex (Bao et al., 2001), suggesting that the phenomenon observed here in the T1 conditioning paradigm may represent the neurophysiological basis for dynamic neural events.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bao et al., 2001).

claim: The phenomenon observed in the T1 conditioning paradigm may represent the neurophysiological basis for dynamic neural events.
source: In fact, it is known that DA release plays a major role in dynamic cortical remodeling in the auditory cortex (Bao et al., 2001), suggesting that the phenomenon observed here in the T1 conditioning paradigm may represent the neurophysiological basis for dynamic neural events.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the experimental results and comparison with auditory cortex findings.

claim: PFC neurons show long-lasting Ca2+ transients that depend on the D1 receptor pathway.
source: Besides network modification in PFC, it has also been demonstrated that PFC neurons show long-lasting Ca2+ transients that depend on the D1 receptor pathway.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: Association learning is only successful if the cue signal is less than 20–30 s before the reward signal.
source: For example, association learning is only successful if the cue signal is less than 20–30 s before the reward signal.
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge about association learning.

claim: Long-lasting Ca2+ transients may be tightly associated with the time window in association learning.
source: Long-lasting Ca2+ transients may be tightly associated with this time window in association learning.
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the observed Ca2+ transients to the known time window for association learning.

claim: Long-lasting Ca2+ transients could be a key phenomenon required to explain the dynamics of the dopaminergic neural network and its role in PFC cognitive functions.
source: Taken together, the long-lasting Ca2+ transients reported here could be a key phenomenon required to explain the dynamics of the dopaminergic neural network and its role in PFC cognitive functions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a broader significance of the findings.

claim: Dopamine is critical for higher neural processes and modifying the activity of the prefrontal cortex (PFC).
source: Dopamine is critical for higher neural processes and modifying the activity of the prefrontal cortex (PFC).
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Phasic stimulation of dopaminergic neurons in the VTA evokes prolonged Ca2+ transients, lasting ∼30 s in layer 2/3 neurons of the PFC.
source: Phasic stimulation of dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) evoked prolonged Ca2+ transients, lasting ∼30 s in layer 2/3 neurons of the PFC, which are regulated by a dopamine D1 receptor-dependent pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the manuscript.

claim: Prolonged Ca2+ transients in layer 2/3 neurons of the PFC are regulated by a dopamine D1 receptor-dependent pathway.
source: Phasic stimulation of dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) evoked prolonged Ca2+ transients, lasting ∼30 s in layer 2/3 neurons of the PFC, which are regulated by a dopamine D1 receptor-dependent pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Only a conditioning protocol with visual sensory input applied 0.5 s before the VTA dopaminergic input could evoke enhanced Ca2+ transients and increased pattern similarity of PFC neurons to the same sensory input.
source: Furthermore, only a conditioning protocol with visual sensory input applied 0.5 s before the VTA dopaminergic input could evoke enhanced Ca2+ transients and increased pattern similarity (or establish a neural representation) of PFC neurons to the same sensory input.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the conditioning experiments.

claim: By increasing both the level of neuronal response and pattern similarity, dopaminergic input may establish robust and reliable cortical representation.
source: By increasing both the level of neuronal response and pattern similarity, dopaminergic input may establish robust and reliable cortical representation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and presented as a conclusion.

claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays an important role in adaptive behavior such as associative learning.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays an important role in adaptive behavior such as associative learning (Duncan, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Duncan, 2001).

claim: Dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) is crucial for PFC function.
source: Dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) is crucial for PFC function (Schultz, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Schultz, 2007).

claim: In primates, sensory cues used in associative learning tasks create specific temporal activity patterns in PFC neurons and a neural representation of the sensory cue.
source: In primates, sensory cues, which are used in associative learning tasks, create specific temporal activity patterns in PFC neurons and a neural representation of the sensory cue (Jacob et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Jacob et al., 2013).

claim: Dopaminergic (DA) neurons target dopamine over a number of inhibitory and excitatory neurons via their widespread axonal arborizations.
source: One potential mechanism is that dopaminergic (DA) neurons target dopamine over a number of inhibitory and excitatory neurons via their widespread axonal arborizations (Matsuda et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Matsuda et al., 2009).

claim: Approximately 50–80 cells were analyzed in each animal.
source: Approximately 50–80 cells were analyzed in each animal.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Population average of Ca2+ transients in response to 10 pulses at 50 Hz VTA stimulation shows clear response in awake mice but not in mice under anesthesia.
source: Population average of Ca2+ transients (dF/F) in response to 10 pulses at 50 Hz VTA stimulation (n = 4 animals). VTA electrical stimulation was applied at the 30 s time point (red arrowhead). In contrast to a clear response in awake mice (left), the long-lasting Ca2+ transients were not detected in mice under anesthesia (right, 4% isoflurane).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The same animals were used for the 'Awake' and 'Under anesthesia' experiments.
source: The same animals were used for the 'Awake' and 'Under anesthesia' experiments.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claim: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA with temporal change and conditioning paradigm as factors revealed significant differences in temporal change (F(3, 84) = 48.486, p < 0.0001) and the conditioning paradigm × temporal change interaction (F(9,84) = 3.173, p = 0.0024).
source: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA with temporal change (before, right after, 1 hr after, and 2 hr after conditioning) and conditioning paradigm (V2L only, VTA only, Timing1, and Timing2) as factors, revealed that population averages of dF/F values of Ca2+ transients signal showed significant differences in temporal change (F(3, 84) = 48.486, p < 0.0001) and the conditioning paradigm × temporal change interaction (F(9,84) = 3.173, p = 0.0024) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA on the temporal changes of the mean cosine similarities in each conditioning paradigm revealed significant differences in the temporal factor (F(3, 84) = 7.676, p = 0.0001) and the time × condition paradigm interaction (F(9, 84) = 2.483, p = 0.0145).
source: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA on the temporal changes of the mean cosine similarities in each conditioning paradigm revealed significant differences in the temporal factor (F(3, 84) = 7.676, p = 0.0001) and the time × condition paradigm interaction (F(9, 84) = 2.483, p = 0.0145; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.
